parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.

parent.name: Vienna Game
parent.overview: White develops the queen's knight before the king's knight, protecting e4 and adding a second guard of d5, and keeps the f-pawn free. That flexibility is the point: White can later play f4 for a delayed King's Gambit (the Vienna Gambit), develop the bishop with 3.Bc4 for an Italian or Bishop's Opening structure (with the Qg4 raid against ...Bc5 and the Frankenstein-Dracula after ...Nxe4), or fianchetto with 3.g3 for a quieter game. Black usually answers 2...Nf6 (the Falkbeer, about 60 percent in one source) or 2...Nc6, and the standard equaliser is a timely ...d5. Theory leaves the opening objectively equal, with little elite use but a lot of club use; it is a surprise weapon that avoids the heavily prepared Spanish and Italian lines. The root is a family, so its character depends on White's third move.

parent.name: Bishop's Opening
parent.overview: White develops the bishop to c4 at once, eyeing f7 and discouraging ...d5, while keeping the f-pawn free for f4 and delaying the knight on g1. Unlike the Italian, White does not commit a knight to f3 on move two, so the opening is highly transpositional: after 2...Nc6 it tends to become an Italian or Vienna, after 2...Nf6 White usually plays 3.d3 (or the sharp Urusov Gambit 3.d4), and after 2...Bc5 play is symmetrical and can reach a Giuoco Piano. Theory judges it equal with best play. At master level it is a surprise weapon used to avoid Petrov preparation, not a main line.

parent.name: Philidor Defense
parent.overview: Black defends e5 with the d-pawn instead of the knight, building a compact centre at the cost of space and piece mobility. Wikipedia calls it solid but passive (s1); the dark-squared bishop and sometimes the whole position can be cramped (s2, s4). The usual game is White taking space after 3.d4 or developing with 3.Bc4, and Black setting up the Hanham formation (...Nf6, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...c6, ...O-O), then freeing the position by ...exd4 or ...d5 at the right moment (s1, s4). Modern analysis finds it dynamically balanced, not just passive (s3). Strong players use it rarely; Wikipedia says no top player used it regularly as of 2017, though it has grown in rapid, blitz and bullet (s1). Move orders matter: Black must avoid several tactical pitfalls (s2, s4).

parent.name: Ruy Lopez
parent.overview: The Ruy Lopez is the most extensively developed Open Game. 3.Bb5 attacks the knight that defends e5, building indirect pressure on the e5 pawn without the Italian's vulnerability to ...d5. This root (3.Bb5) is a crossroads: after the most common 3...a6 (about two-thirds of games) the Closed Spanish (4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3) leads to a slow, locked-centre manoeuvring game; the Berlin (3...Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4) gives a solid, drawish endgame-flavoured structure; the Marshall Attack is a sharp Black pawn sacrifice. White's central plan is c3 and d4 plus the Nbd2-f1-g3 knight route, while Black counterattacks on the queenside (...b5, ...Na5, ...c5) or breaks with ...d5. Theory is the deepest of any 1.e4 opening.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.e4 with ...c5 to trade a flank pawn for White's d-pawn, which leaves Black a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file in return for White's lead in development and space. This asymmetry is the point: Black plays for a win rather than equality. The usual pattern is White attacking on the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside along the c-file (...b5, ...Rc8), often with opposite-side castling in the sharpest lines. The root is a crossroads: after 2.Nf3 (about 80% of master games, s1) it branches into Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen, Classical, Sveshnikov, Taimanov and Kan, which range from forcing and theory-heavy (Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov) to flexible and solid (Kan, Classical, Taimanov). White's anti-Sicilians (Alapin, Closed, Grand Prix, 2.d3) avoid the Open Sicilian and are quieter. The root as a whole is the most played and most analysed opening at club and master level (s1).

parent.name: Center Game
parent.overview: White strikes the centre at once: 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 regains the pawn and opens the game, at the cost of an early queen that Black hits with 3...Nc6. The queen goes to e3 (Paulsen's Attack, 4.Qe3), and White develops quickly with Nc3, Bd2, Bc4 or Be2, castles queenside and aims the queen and the semi-open d-file at g7 and the kingside, or pushes the h-pawn. Black has calm, sound set-ups (4...Nf6, 4...Be7 preparing ...d5, 4...g6, 4...Bb4+) and equalises with accurate play. Opposite-side castling can turn it into a race. Instead of 3.Qxd4, White can play 3.c3 (Danish Gambit), which is a separate gambit branch.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: French Variation
parent.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4
parent.overview: 2...e6 is a gateway rather than a set-up: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black chooses the Taimanov (...Nc6), the Kan (...a6) or the Scheveningen (...d6, ...Nf6), with 3.Nc3 giving the Paulsen/Kan/Taimanov move orders. Black opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5 or ...Nc6/...a6 in a flexible way, with a solid ...e6/...d6 pawn chain and queenside counterplay. The name 'French' is only a naming convention: the pawn structure is Sicilian, not a French one. White's main choice is 3.d4 (about 61% of moves at 2500); rarer third moves are 3.d3, 3.g3, 3.c3 and Westerinen's 3.b3 (Bb2, occasional in the 1970s). At higher levels play is heavily theoretical.

parent.name: Scandinavian Defense: Mieses-Kotroc Variation
parent.overview: After 2...Qxd5 Black recaptures at once, gaining the pawn back but exposing the queen: White's 3.Nc3 hits it with a tempo and Black must move it again, usually 3...Qa5 (the Mieses-Kotroc proper), 3...Qd6 or 3...Qd8. Black then builds a Caro-Kann-like structure with ...c6, ...Nf6, ...Bf5 (or ...Bg4) and ...e6, aiming for central breaks with ...c5 or ...e5 and pressure on the semi-open c- and d-files. White keeps a small lead in development and a space edge, and wins nothing material if Black plays accurately. Sources describe it as solid and positional rather than sharp, low in theory, with plans that repeat from game to game, which makes it popular with club players and improvers; the drawbacks are a small space deficit and early queen exposure with traps to avoid. It is the most popular and most analysed Scandinavian line, used by Carlsen and others.

parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.

parent.name: Petrov's Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 2.Nf3 by counter-attacking e4 rather than defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 both sides have lost an e-pawn and the structure is symmetrical, with the e-file the main open line. Black's aim is to equalise by quick development and piece trades; White tries to turn a small lead in development or slightly freer play into pressure, often castling and using the e-file or a queenside castling and pawn storm. The 3.d4 Steinitz line (3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 Nd7) and 3.Nc3 (Four Knights transposition) or 3.d3 sidelines give quieter or more varied structures. The main lines are widely played at the top and are known as drawish, though some lines hold real attacking chances for both sides.
